slides.title: Keep connector C: redesign it now, fix bundle service, and decide any 2029 sunset on evidence

paragraphs.text: Keep connector C: redesign it now, fix bundle service, and decide any 2029 sunset on evidence
Board question: should Vesper discontinue low reported-margin sterile connector C and redeploy the team to connector D?
Pre-read for the February 2027 board meeting  |  Prepared November 2026
All figures in US$ millions, FY2026 full year, from the board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data)

slides.title: Do not discontinue C in 2027: exiting would destroy cash and breach board constraints. Redesign C, fix bundle service, and make any sunset a 2029 decision

paragraphs.text: Do not discontinue C in 2027: exiting would destroy cash and breach board constraints. Redesign C, fix bundle service, and make any sunset a 2029 decision
C's 8% margin comes from the cost allocation; C is actually the portfolio's highest-contribution connector
C earns $3.8M direct contribution, a 63% contribution margin vs 50% for D, 50% for A and 42% for B
Only $0.4M of C's $3.3M allocated cost is avoidable; the other $2.9M would move onto A, B and D
Exiting C in 2027 loses $4.75M in the first year and $2.65M every year after, and breaks two non-negotiables
Even if D wins the optimistic 25% of C revenue, D adds only $0.75M; break-even would need $6.8M of D sales (113% of C)
The $2.1M penalty alone is 2.3x the $0.9M cash envelope; C sits in 9 of 14 major bundles with no validated substitute
The customer case for exit does not hold up: the real problem is bundle fill, caused by A and B
The 9-point renewal gap is confounded by hospital size, legacy equipment and customer-success coverage; there is no before/after test
C's 98% on-time figure leaves out bundle misses caused by A and B. Bundle fill is 91% vs the 95% contracted, and exiting C would not fix it
Recommended: redesign C now (+$2.4M over 2027–29), recover bundle fill, then hand the team to D
The $0.55M redesign pays back in ~5 months of savings and still breaks even at 19% of the $1.25M estimate; it fits within the $0.9M
Renew the two bundles without exit notice and with a consent-based D path; hold a Q4 2028 gate on a 2029 sunset
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Sections A–D of this deck follow these four points.

slides.title: Our starting hypothesis, "keep C", survived four of five tests; the fifth showed that keeping C unchanged is not enough

paragraphs.text: Our starting hypothesis, "keep C", survived four of five tests; the fifth showed that keeping C unchanged is not enough
Initial hypothesis (set before testing): Vesper should retain C, because its low reported margin is an allocation effect rather than an avoidable economic cost.
What would have to be true
C earns more cash than its exit would save
C direct contribution $3.8M vs avoidable fixed cost $0.4M, so exit gives up a net $3.4M a year before any migration
D cannot replace what C earns
Migration ceiling 25% of C revenue = $1.5M (all of D's spare capacity) x 50% = $0.75M, vs $3.4M at stake
$2.1M first-year penalties vs $0.9M approved cash; C sits in 9 of 14 major bundles and no substitute is validated across every hospital model
C is not driving customer attrition
The 9-point renewal gap is correlational and confounded (size, legacy equipment, CS coverage); there is no before/after evidence either way
Bundle fill is 91% vs 95% required; C faces price pressure; a $1.25M a year redesign saving is available for $0.55M

Revised answer: Keep C, but not unchanged. Fund the C redesign, bring bundle fill back to 95%, use the renewals to open a consent-based path to D, and treat a 2029 sunset as a decision for Q4 2028, made on observed evidence. Test 4 stays open, and the plan includes a way to resolve it.

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Verdict colours carry labels; blue = supports hypothesis, amber = evidence inconclusive, red = hypothesis needs refining.

slides.title: C's 8% "gross margin" comes from the allocation: C earns $3.8M of direct contribution, and only $0.4M of its $3.3M allocated cost would go away if C exits

paragraphs.text: C's 8% "gross margin" comes from the allocation: C earns $3.8M of direct contribution, and only $0.4M of its $3.3M allocated cost would go away if C exits
Connector C, FY2026, $M: walk from sales to reported profit
Two different margins. Reported margin = (6.0 – 2.2 – 3.3) / 6.0 = 8.3%. Contribution margin = 3.8 / 6.0 = 63.3%.
88% of the allocation stays. $2.9M of the $3.3M is shared regulatory documentation and plant depreciation, spread by historical engineering hours. It does not go away when the SKU does.
Exit decisions turn on $3.4M. Exiting C removes $3.8M of contribution and saves $0.4M of fixed cost, so Vesper loses $3.4M a year before any migration to D.
The dashboard label misleads. The figure called "product gross margin" is measured after shared allocations, so it cannot be used to rank products for an exit or capacity decision.
$3.4M a year of profit lost on exit, not 8%
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Avoidable fixed cost of $0.40M per Finance; direct variable cost is fully avoidable if shipments end.

slides.title: On contribution, C is Vesper's strongest connector (63% vs D's 50%), and exiting it would move $2.9M of stranded cost onto A, B and D

paragraphs.text: On contribution, C is Vesper's strongest connector (63% vs D's 50%), and exiting it would move $2.9M of stranded cost onto A, B and D
Margin by product, FY2026, % of sales
If C exits: illustrative reported margins once $2.9M is reallocated

Implication: the stranded cost does not go away when C does; it lands on A, B and D. B's reported margin would fall to about 17%, and the same margin-ranking logic would then pick B as the next "weakest" product. Total allocated cost falls by only $0.4M (from 6.5 to 6.1).

Allocation basis: the pack says the remaining cost "would move to A, B and D" but does not give the split. We assume it moves pro rata to today's allocation (1.2 : 1.2 : 0.8). D's figure includes $1.5M of migrated revenue at 50% contribution.

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Contribution margin = (sales – direct variable cost) / sales. Reported margin = (sales – variable – allocated) / sales.

slides.title: Exiting C cuts cash contribution by $4.75M in its first year and $2.65M every year after, even if D wins the optimistic 25% of C revenue

paragraphs.text: B  |  WHAT WOULD EXITING C COST?
Exiting C cuts cash contribution by $4.75M in its first year and $2.65M every year after, even if D wins the optimistic 25% of C revenue
Exit bridge vs retaining C, first 12 months after exit, $M
Operating profit after allocations, $M a year
Penalties are one-time. Following Finance, the $2.1M is treated as a first-year cost, not recurring overhead. Even with every penalty waived, exit still loses $2.65M a year.
Migration is a ceiling, not a forecast. The 25% comes from three sales interviews. It needs customer-specific adapters and validation.
Not yet costed: replacement qualification, clinical documentation, and any A/B accounts lost with the bundle.
D migration at ceiling (25% x $6.0M x 50%)

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Operating profit = total contribution 16.6 – allocated fixed 6.5. Exit case: contribution 16.6 – 3.8 + 0.75; fixed 6.5 – 0.4.

slides.title: No migration rate makes exit pay: even if every C customer moved to D, Vesper would still lose $0.4M a year, and D can take only 25% today

paragraphs.text: B  |  WHAT WOULD EXITING C COST?
No migration rate makes exit pay: even if every C customer moved to D, Vesper would still lose $0.4M a year, and D can take only 25% today
Recurring annual impact of exit, by share of C revenue migrating to D, $M
of migrated D revenue needed to offset the $3.4M lost each year ($3.4M ÷ 50%). That is 113% of C's entire $6.0M revenue and 4.5x D's spare capacity.
Why D cannot close the gap: C's contribution margin (63%) is higher than D's incremental 50%, so each dollar moved from C to D earns less.
Migration crowds out D growth: the 25% ceiling would use all of D's $1.5M spare capacity, leaving no room for D's own organic growth.
The 25% is unobserved: it is the portfolio team's ceiling from three interviews. Finance has not estimated any recapture beyond it.
Above D's current capacity: needs new D capacity and a validated adapter at every account

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Bars beyond 25% (light, dashed) are hypothetical and exceed D's current capacity. Excludes the one-time $2.1M penalty.

slides.title: A 2027 exit would also break the board's non-negotiables: the penalty alone is 2.3x the approved cash, and C is in 9 of 14 major hospital bundles

paragraphs.text: B  |  WHAT WOULD EXITING C COST?
A 2027 exit would also break the board's non-negotiables: the penalty alone is 2.3x the approved cash, and C is in 9 of 14 major hospital bundles
What a Q2 2027 exit of C would do

9 of 14 major hospital relationships specify a bundle containing C alongside A and B. No substitute for C has completed validation across every hospital model, so removing C leaves those bundles incomplete. Fill is already 91%.
First-year bundle penalties of $2.1M are payable unless counterparties consent. Replacement qualification and clinical documentation come on top and have not been costed.
Exit requires notice, replacement qualification and clinical documentation. Two bundle agreements are being renewed now, so an exit notice would go into live negotiations.
Judge on cash contribution, not the allocation report
Cash contribution falls by $3.4M a year before migration and $2.65M after the 25% ceiling, plus the $2.1M penalty in year one.
Implication: a 2027 exit cannot go ahead without the board relaxing at least two of its own constraints. No other option on the table requires that (see page 12).

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Assumes the $2.1M penalty counts against the 2027 one-time cash envelope because it is a direct cash consequence of the portfolio change.

slides.title: Moving the team to D cannot replace C: D's spare capacity caps the upside at $0.75M a year, and Vesper can capture that without exiting C

paragraphs.text: B  |  WHAT WOULD EXITING C COST?
Moving the team to D cannot replace C: D's spare capacity caps the upside at $0.75M a year, and Vesper can capture that without exiting C
Engineering capacity: what we know and what we don't
Known: D has room for $1.5M more revenue at present capacity. That room exists whether or not C exits. Under an exit, migrating C customers would fill it, crowding out D's own growth.
Known: the C redesign needs one design team for about four months (validation phase), then hands the team back.
Not known: the pack gives no quantified opportunity cost for those four months, and we do not invent one.

Illustrative ceiling only: suppose the team's absence delayed filling D's spare capacity by the full four months. The cost would then be at most 4/12 x $0.75M ≈ $0.25M, against $1.25M a year of redesign savings.
Answer to "redeploy to D?": yes, but in sequence. The team works on the C redesign from March to June 2027 and moves to D (adapter validation and growth) from July.
Most D can add at present capacity
C's economics are 4.5x the most D can add without new capacity
D's "30% margin" is also after allocations. D's incremental contribution at existing capacity is 50%, still below C's 63%.
Growth is not replacement. D's double-digit market growth adds value at the margin. It does not justify giving up $3.8M of existing contribution (Finance's point).
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). The $0.25M is a bound under a stated assumption, not an estimate of lost D sales.

slides.title: The 9-point renewal gap does not show C causes churn: C buyers are smaller, legacy-equipment, lower-coverage accounts, and nothing tests what removing C would do

paragraphs.text: The 9-point renewal gap does not show C causes churn: C buyers are smaller, legacy-equipment, lower-coverage accounts, and nothing tests what removing C would do
The CEO's claim and the factors it does not control for
Verdict and the test the board should require
Correlation, not causation. C accounts differ systematically in size, equipment age and service coverage. Each of these could lower renewal on its own.
No counterfactual. The sample has no before/after evidence that removing C raises retention. It cannot support exit, and it cannot rule out a C effect either.
Tests to run before the Q4 2028 gate:
Compare renewal within matched segments (size x equipment age x CS coverage)
Control for bundle fill each account actually received
Code lost-account exit reasons for any mention of C
Track retention of any accounts that drop C or move to D
Decision rule: only a renewal gap that persists within segments should feed the sunset decision, and then it should be valued against the $3.4M a year C contributes.
Bundle fill 91%, caused by A/B misses (our hypothesis, untested)
Grey boxes: confounders named in the briefing pack. Amber: a further plausible confounder. The 9 C-bundle customers are the ones receiving 91% fill, but the pack does not link this to renewals.
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data).

slides.title: The real service problem is bundle fill, at 91% against 95% contracted; A and B misses cause it and the C dashboard hides it, so exiting C would not fix it

paragraphs.text: The real service problem is bundle fill, at 91% against 95% contracted; A and B misses cause it and the C dashboard hides it, so exiting C would not fix it
Fix the measure and the misses, not C
Redefine the KPI: make bundle-level contracted fill the headline service metric for every bundle customer. Report product-level fill only as a diagnostic.
Root-cause the A and B misses on the nine bundle accounts. Size buffer stock or allocation priority for A and B in those bundles.
Report monthly to the board until fill has stayed at 95% or above for two consecutive quarters.
Unknown: recovery speed. The pack does not say how fast bundle service can recover or what that costs. We have set a Q3 2027 target as a working assumption for Operations to confirm in February.
Note: axis starts at 85% to show the gap; values are labelled.
The dashboard definition: C's 98% counts C as filled even when the bundle ships late because A or B is missing. The contract measures complete bundles, and that figure is 91%.
The cause sits in A and B, not C. Exiting C leaves the A/B misses in place and makes the nine C-bundles incomplete.
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data).

slides.title: Redesigning C is the only option that adds value and meets every constraint: +$2.4M over 2027–29, against –$8.7M for an immediate exit

paragraphs.text: D  |  WHAT SHOULD VESPER DO INSTEAD?
Redesigning C is the only option that adds value and meets every constraint: +$2.4M over 2027–29, against –$8.7M for an immediate exit
Needs A/B fix; time to validate adapter
A/B bundle volume at risk (unquantified); B next 'weakest'
Price pressure erodes C; $1.25M saving forgone
As retain; locks in high-cost C until 2029
Requalification delay at 2 customers; savings below estimate

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Timing: exit effective 1 Jul 2027 (2027 loses half-year contribution, full $2.1M penalty); redesign savings from 1 Sep 2027 after validation and pilot. Migration at the 25% ceiling.

slides.title: The $0.55M redesign pays back in about 5 months of savings and still breaks even if it delivers only a fifth of the $1.25M estimate

paragraphs.text: D  |  WHAT SHOULD VESPER DO INSTEAD?
The $0.55M redesign pays back in about 5 months of savings and still breaks even if it delivers only a fifth of the $1.25M estimate
Of estimated savings needed to break even by 2029
50% of savings, 3 months late, full $0.9M envelope spent
Redesign scenarios: cash contribution vs retain unchanged, $M
C's reported margin rises to ~29%, level with D's 30%, if the $1.25M comes out of direct cost: (6.0 – 0.95 – 3.3) / 6.0. The ranking that started this debate goes away.
Operating profit rises 12%, from $10.1M to $11.35M a year at full run-rate.
Caution: $1.25M equals 57% of C's $2.2M direct cost, an engineering estimate at current volume. The two-site pilot exists to test it before the whole line converts.
Base: $1.25M a year from Sep 2027; $0.55M cost
Downside: $0.63M a year from Dec 2027; $0.90M cost
Break-even: $0.24M a year from Sep 2027; $0.55M cost
Break-even with full $0.9M spent: $0.39M a year
Rounded. 2027 savings run Sep–Dec (4 months); window = 28 months = 2.33 years. Downside 2027: –0.90 + 0.63 x 1/12. Break-even rows solve for the savings that make the 2027–29 total zero.

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Redesign cost excludes possible requalification tests at two customers; the downside case uses the $0.35M remaining in the envelope for them.

slides.title: Use the two renewals to secure C supply, bundle-level service terms and a consent-based path to D, not to give exit notice

paragraphs.text: D  |  WHAT SHOULD VESPER DO INSTEAD?
Use the two renewals to secure C supply, bundle-level service terms and a consent-based path to D, not to give exit notice
Renew with C in the bundle; give no exit notice
Add a clause allowing substitution by a validated D + adapter only with customer consent, after qualification
Align term end with the 2029 expiry cohort so any sunset can happen at expiry, without penalty
Q1 2027; terms set at Feb board
Confirm C supply through current terms
Pre-notify the C design change and agree requalification tests early with the two customers that need them
Make bundle-level fill the contract KPI on every service dashboard
Root-cause A/B misses; set A/B buffer or allocation priority for bundle accounts; report monthly until ≥95%
Carry the $2.1M as a contingent one-time liability tied to premature termination, not as annual overhead (Finance's rule)
Run adapter and quality qualification with willing C customers; record actual acceptance, not interview estimates

Why this order: the penalty stands unless counterparties consent, so consent-based substitution and expiry-aligned terms are the only routes to a penalty-free exit later. Fixing A/B fill protects all nine bundles whatever happens to C.

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Leads, and the Q3 2027 fill target, are proposals for management to confirm; the pack names neither owners nor a recovery date.

slides.title: A staged plan with two decision gates protects $3.8M of contribution today and keeps a 2029 sunset open if the evidence turns

paragraphs.text: D  |  WHAT SHOULD VESPER DO INSTEAD?
A staged plan with two decision gates protects $3.8M of contribution today and keeps a 2029 sunset open if the evidence turns
Full line at run-rate savings (from Sep 2027)
On D: adapter validation and D growth
Bundle terms run; requalification with 2 customers
Only if Gate 2 passes: migrate at expiry
Gate 1, end of Aug 2027: convert the whole C line?
Go if the pilot run-rate saving is ≥$0.4M a year (the break-even with the full $0.9M spent) and no customer requalification has failed
Otherwise stop at the pilot sites, with spend capped inside the $0.9M envelope
Gate 2, Q4 2028 (or the notice deadline, if earlier): sunset C in 2029?

Consider sunset only if: D adapter validated on every hospital model in C bundles; observed acceptance high enough; D capacity in place; fill ≥95% for 2 quarters; renewal gap shown to be causal; updated exit bridge positive

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). Assumes redesign kick-off in Mar 2027, 4-month validation, 2-month pilot. Contract notice periods are not in the pack; Gate 2 must precede them.

slides.title: None of the open unknowns is likely to flip the decision against exit, and each is tested at a gate in the plan

paragraphs.text: D  |  WHAT SHOULD VESPER DO INSTEAD?
None of the open unknowns is likely to flip the decision against exit, and each is tested at a gate in the plan
25% is a ceiling from three sales interviews; adapters and validation are customer-specific
None: even 100% migration loses $0.4M a year
Not included in the $0.55M; could delay savings

Low: breaks even at 19% of estimate (31% if the full $0.9M is spent)

Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data). C price-pressure threshold: exit run-rate = –C contribution + 0.4 + 0.75 = 0, so C contribution = $1.15M.

slides.title: We ask the board for six decisions that keep $3.8M of contribution, avoid $2.1M of penalties and add about $1.25M a year

paragraphs.text: We ask the board for six decisions that keep $3.8M of contribution, avoid $2.1M of penalties and add about $1.25M a year
Exit loses $4.75M in year one and $2.65M a year after, and breaches the cash and fill constraints
Approve $0.55M for the C redesign, plus up to $0.35M reserve, within the $0.9M envelope
Pilot at two sites first; Gate 1 at end of Aug 2027
Mandate bundle-level contracted fill as the service KPI
Operations to present an A/B recovery plan to reach ≥95%, with dates and cost
Authorise renewal terms for the two bundle agreements
C retained; consent-based D substitution clause; terms aligned to 2029 expiries
Sequence engineering: C redesign Mar–Jun 2027, then D
The D adapter work also builds the evidence for any later sunset
Set Gate 2 criteria for any 2029 sunset (Q4 2028)
Validated adapter, observed acceptance, sustained ≥95% fill, causal renewal test, positive exit bridge
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data).

slides.title: Every number in the deck comes from briefing-pack inputs with the arithmetic shown here

paragraphs.text: Every number in the deck comes from briefing-pack inputs with the arithmetic shown here
Contribution margin = (sales – direct variable) / sales: A 7.0/14.0 = 50.0%; B 3.8/9.0 = 42.2%; C 3.8/6.0 = 63.3%; D 2.0/4.0 = 50.0%
Reported margin = (sales – variable – allocated) / sales: A 5.8/14.0 = 41.4%; B 2.6/9.0 = 28.9%; C 0.5/6.0 = 8.3%; D 1.2/4.0 = 30.0%
Break-even migrated D revenue = 3.4 / 0.5 = 6.8 = 113% of C sales, 4.5x D spare capacity of 1.5
Operating profit after exit: 16.6 – 3.8 + 0.75 = 13.55 contribution – 6.1 fixed = 7.45 (–26%); no migration 6.7 (–34%)
Reallocation if C exits (pro rata assumption)
Reported C margin after redesign = (6.0 – 0.95 – 3.3)/6.0 = 29.2%; operating profit 10.1 + 1.25 = 11.35 (+12%)
Engineering ceiling = 4/12 x 0.75 = 0.25; C price-pressure break-even: 3.8 – 1.15 = 2.65 drop (70%)
Source: Vesper MedTech board briefing pack (FY2026 full-year figures; synthetic data).
